To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the dissipation strength of the compound nuclei 210Rn, 212Rn, 214Rn, 216Rn, populated in the reactions of 16, 18O+194Pt, 198Pt, at excitation energies between 50 and 79 MeVs, shows N/Z dependence in the low energy region, but not at higher energies.
the N/Z dependence of neutron multiplicity in the pre-scission stage of the fission process is observed only at lowest excitation energies.

the neutron multiplicity data of 210,212, 214, 216 Rn compound nuclei are measured for the first time, and their statistical model analysis shows that shell effect is observed at the lowest excitation energies of the compound nuclei but not observed at higher excitation energies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of the neutron/proton ratio (N/Z) on nuclear dissipation.
the effect of neutron/proton ratio in pre-scission neutrons and the fission time scale for 210,212 Rn and 214,216 R.
the study of the N/Z dependence of fission dynamics in compound nuclei with N/Z values varying from 1.4 to 1.5.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a strong N/Z dependence of dissipation strength at low excitation energy and this effect is not observed at high excitation energy.
the dissipation strength is not constant with N/Z.
the N/Z variation of the fission time scale in the region of the heaviest nuclei is not a monotonic function of N/Z.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the variation of N/Z with the fission time scale shows the shell closure effects at lowest excitations, however, such effects are smeared out at higher excitations.
the variation of the N/Z in pre-fission neutron multiplicities is not only governed by the dissipation strength but also by the excitation energy of compound nucleus.
the N/Z effect is observed at low excitation energy but not at high excitation energy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the N/Z dependence of dissipation strength is not a monotonic function of N/Z.
the dissipation strength is a strong function of excitation energy and the dissipation is more pronounced at low excitation energies.
the dissipation strength in the compound nuclei 210 Rn and 212 Rn are found to be different.
